**Pattern 565: WDIO v9 `element.getComputedLabel()` + `getComputedRole()` for Automated Accessibility Audit in Mobile WebViews** [official]
Regression-testing ARIA accessibility properties on mobile WebViews is often skipped because accessibility tree inspection requires expensive screen-reader integration. WDIO v9's `element.getComputedLabel()` and `element.getComputedRole()` (backed by the WebDriver Accessibility API) return the computed ARIA label and role without enabling a screen reader, enabling fast in-band accessibility checks.
```typescript
// helpers/a11y-check.ts
export interface A11yAssertion {
  selector: string;
  expectedRole: string;
  expectedLabel?: string | RegExp;
}

export async function assertA11yProperties(
  assertions: A11yAssertion[]
): Promise<void> {
  const failures: string[] = [];

  for (const { selector, expectedRole, expectedLabel } of assertions) {
    const el = await $(selector);
    const [role, label] = await Promise.all([
      el.getComputedRole(),
      el.getComputedLabel(),
    ]);

    if (role !== expectedRole) {
      failures.push(`${selector}: expected role "${expectedRole}", got "${role}"`);
    }
    if (expectedLabel !== undefined) {
      const matches = expectedLabel instanceof RegExp
        ? expectedLabel.test(label)
        : label === expectedLabel;
      if (!matches) {
        failures.push(`${selector}: expected label "${expectedLabel}", got "${label}"`);
      }
    }
  }

  if (failures.length > 0) {
    throw new Error(`Accessibility violations:\n${failures.join('\n')}`);
  }
}

// spec.ts
it('product page meets ARIA requirements', async () => {
  await browser.switchContext('WEBVIEW_com.example.app');
  await browser.url('/products/42');

  await assertA11yProperties([
    { selector: '[data-testid="add-to-cart"]', expectedRole: 'button', expectedLabel: /add.*cart/i },
    { selector: '[data-testid="product-image"]', expectedRole: 'img', expectedLabel: /product photo/i },
    { selector: '[data-testid="price-display"]', expectedRole: 'text', expectedLabel: /\$\d+/ },
    { selector: 'nav[aria-label]', expectedRole: 'navigation' },
  ]);
});
```
Tradeoff: `getComputedRole()` and `getComputedLabel()` are WebDriver Accessibility API endpoints — they require the underlying browser engine to implement the spec (Chrome 92+, Safari 15.4+). Older system WebView versions on Android devices with API < 31 may return `''` (empty string) for both properties because the WebView's ChromeDriver does not expose the Accessibility API. `getComputedLabel()` does not account for off-screen `aria-hidden` — a button hidden with `aria-hidden="true"` returns an empty label (correct), but a button visually hidden via `opacity: 0` or `transform: scale(0)` returns the actual label (expected behavior but can cause false positives in visual regression checks). These APIs are WebView-only; there is no native Appium equivalent for XCUI/UIAutomator2 accessibility trees — use `mobile: getPageSource()` XML parsing for native layer inspection.

---

**Pattern 566: Appium 2 `driver.setOrientation()` + `waitUntil` for Orientation-Change Animation Completion Synchronization** [official]
`driver.setOrientation('LANDSCAPE')` returns as soon as the rotation command is dispatched — the device animation completes asynchronously (approximately 350–600 ms depending on device and OS). Tests that interact with elements immediately after rotation fail intermittently because layout recalculation has not completed by the time the element query fires.
```typescript
// helpers/orientation.ts
export type DeviceOrientation = 'PORTRAIT' | 'LANDSCAPE';

export async function rotateDevice(
  targetOrientation: DeviceOrientation,
  stabilizeTimeoutMs = 3000
): Promise<void> {
  const currentOrientation = await driver.getOrientation();
  if (currentOrientation === targetOrientation) return;

  await driver.setOrientation(targetOrientation);

  // Wait for layout recalculation by polling window dimensions
  const isLandscape = targetOrientation === 'LANDSCAPE';
  await browser.waitUntil(
    async () => {
      const { width, height } = await browser.getWindowSize();
      return isLandscape ? width > height : height > width;
    },
    {
      timeout: stabilizeTimeoutMs,
      interval: 100,
      timeoutMsg: `Device did not complete rotation to ${targetOrientation} within ${stabilizeTimeoutMs}ms`,
    }
  );

  // Additional settling pause for animation completion
  await browser.pause(200);
}

// spec.ts
it('reflows product grid to 3-column layout in landscape', async () => {
  await rotateDevice('LANDSCAPE');
  const gridItems = await $$('[data-testid^="grid-item-"]');
  // In landscape, verify 3 items visible in first row (flex-wrap layout)
  const firstRowItems = await Promise.all(
    gridItems.slice(0, 3).map(el => el.isDisplayedInViewport())
  );
  expect(firstRowItems.every(Boolean)).toBe(true);
  await rotateDevice('PORTRAIT'); // always restore
});
```
Tradeoff: Polling `getWindowSize()` after `setOrientation()` works reliably for detecting layout completion on Android but is unreliable on iOS simulators running Xcode 15+, where the simulator's screen rotation involves a GPU layer animation that completes before the logical bounds update propagates to XCUITest's coordinate system. On iOS, the additional `browser.pause(200)` is usually sufficient, but on slow M1/M2 Mac CI runners under load, 200 ms may be insufficient — increase to 400 ms for CI. Restoration in `afterEach` is mandatory: leaving the device in landscape orientation causes subsequent tests to query incorrect element coordinates.

---

**Pattern 567: WDIO v9 `browser.mock()` with `filterRequest` for Selective API Response Delay Simulation** [community]
Testing loading states and skeleton screens requires API responses to be delayed — not blocked. WDIO v9's `browser.mock()` `respond()` method with a custom `delay` option simulates slow API responses to validate spinner visibility, timeout handling, and retry logic without spinning up a real slow network.
```typescript
// helpers/api-delay.ts
import type { Mock } from 'webdriverio';

const activeMocks: Mock[] = [];

export async function delayApiEndpoint(
  urlPattern: string,
  delayMs: number,
  fixture: Record<string, unknown>
): Promise<Mock> {
  const mock = await browser.mock(urlPattern, { method: 'GET' });
  mock.respond(fixture, {
    fetchResponse: false,
    statusCode: 200,
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    // WDIO v9.3+ supports `delay` in respond options
    delay: delayMs,
  });
  activeMocks.push(mock);
  return mock;
}

export async function clearApiMocks(): Promise<void> {
  for (const mock of activeMocks) {
    await mock.restore();
  }
  activeMocks.length = 0;
}

// spec.ts
afterEach(async () => { await clearApiMocks(); });

it('shows loading spinner for delayed API response', async () => {
  await browser.switchContext('WEBVIEW_com.example.app');
  await delayApiEndpoint('**/api/products', 2000, { products: [] });

  await browser.url('/products');
  const spinner = await $('[data-testid="loading-spinner"]');
  await expect(spinner).toBeDisplayed({ timeout: 500 });        // appears immediately
  await expect(spinner).not.toBeDisplayed({ timeout: 4000 }); // disappears after response
});
```
Tradeoff: The `delay` option in `mock.respond()` was added in WDIO v9.3 and is not documented in the main API reference — it is implemented via a `setTimeout` wrapper in the BiDi network interception handler. In WDIO versions before v9.3, `delay` is silently ignored and the response fires immediately. Verify your WDIO version before relying on this in CI. The mock `delay` adds to the test's total execution time — a 2000 ms delay × 10 tests = 20 additional seconds per test suite run. Use `process.env.CI === 'true'` guards to apply shorter delays in CI while maintaining realistic delays in local development. Mocks registered with `browser.mock()` are session-scoped and survive context switches — always restore in `afterEach`.

---

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha C54-1: `driver.setOrientation()` silently succeeds on Android emulators with `Accelerometer (Virtual)` sensor lock enabled, leaving orientation unchanged**
When an Android emulator is created with the AVD's "Enable device frame" option and the sensor rotation lock (the padlock icon in the emulator toolbar) is engaged, `driver.setOrientation('LANDSCAPE')` returns success (HTTP 200) but the device stays in portrait because UIAutomator2 sends the `OrientationEventListener` rotation change, which is intercepted and cancelled by the Android `WindowManagerService` when sensor lock is active. The test then queries elements in the wrong orientation without any error.

WHY: UIAutomator2's `setOrientation` implementation calls `UiDevice.setOrientationLandscape()` which fires `ROTATION_90` via a virtual sensor injection. The emulator's AVD sensor lock (`Settings.System.ACCELEROMETER_ROTATION = 0`) causes `WindowManagerService.updateRotationLocked()` to return early without dispatching the rotation event to `PhysicalDisplayRotationController`, so the display never physically rotates. The HTTP success response from UIAutomator2 reflects the sensor injection success (it fired the event), not the display rotation completion. Fix: before each rotation test, call `await driver.execute('mobile: shell', { command: 'settings', args: ['put', 'system', 'accelerometer_rotation', '1'] })` to enable auto-rotate, then call `setOrientation()`.

---

**Gotcha C54-2: XCUITest `element.setValue()` on a `UITextField` inside a `UITableViewCell` intermittently inserts text at the wrong cursor position on iOS 17 when the table view was recently scrolled**
After scrolling a `UITableView` to bring a text field into view, immediately calling `element.setValue('text')` on that field can insert characters in reverse order or at position 0 instead of at the end of any pre-existing text. This appears as correct input in slow environments but fails under faster test execution or on faster Apple Silicon Mac CI runners.

WHY: When `UITableViewCell` reuse is triggered by scrolling, the cell's `UITextField` is recycled and re-used with a new data model. XCUITest's element resolution caches the element's `AXElement` reference at query time. During scrolling, the table view's `UIScrollViewDelegate` dequeues and re-enqueues cells asynchronously, invalidating the cached `AXElement` reference. If `element.setValue()` is called before the cell completes its full layout pass (which includes `UITextField`'s `becomeFirstResponder` setup), XCUITest's internal `typingValue` implementation dispatches key events before the text field's `inputDelegate textWillChange:` is called, causing the cursor to be positioned at index 0 rather than at `endOfDocument`. Fix: call `await element.click()` first to explicitly focus the field and wait for `becomeFirstResponder`, then call `await element.clearValue()` to reset cursor position, then `await element.setValue('text')`.

---

**Gotcha C54-3: WDIO v9 `browser.getCookies()` in a hybrid app WebView context returns an empty array when the WebView uses a custom `WebViewClient` with `shouldInterceptRequest` that strips the `Cookie` header before forwarding requests**
In hybrid Android apps, a custom `WebViewClient.shouldInterceptRequest()` that re-issues fetch requests via OkHttp (a common pattern for certificate pinning or custom auth headers) strips the `Cookie` header from the re-issued request for security reasons. From Appium's perspective the cookies are set (visible in `document.cookie` via `browser.execute()`), but `getCookies()` queries ChromeDriver's CDP `Network.getCookies()` which returns only cookies that were transmitted in actual HTTP request headers — cookies present in the JavaScript context but stripped from forwarded requests appear as missing.

WHY: `browser.getCookies()` is implemented via ChromeDriver's `Network.getCookies()` CDP command, which returns the browser's cookie jar for the current page URL by reading from Chromium's `CookieStore`. In a standard WebView, Chromium's `CookieStore` and `document.cookie` share the same in-memory store, so `getCookies()` returns all cookies. When a `WebViewClient.shouldInterceptRequest()` intercepts and re-issues the request via a native HTTP client (OkHttp), the response from OkHttp is returned as a `WebResourceResponse` — this response path bypasses the Chromium cookie update pipeline, so `Set-Cookie` headers from OkHttp responses are never written back to Chromium's `CookieStore`. The cookies exist in the JavaScript scope only because they were written via `document.cookie` on initial page load before the intercept kicked in. Fix: use `browser.execute(() => document.cookie)` to read the cookie string directly from the JavaScript context instead of relying on `getCookies()`.

---

**Gotcha C54-4: Appium 2 `mobile: installApp` on iOS returns before Springboard has finished registering the app, causing `mobile: activateApp` called immediately after to throw `Application is not installed`**
In a CI pipeline with `before()` hook that installs and immediately launches a test app, `mobile: activateApp` (or `driver.activateApp()`) occasionally throws `Error: Application com.example.app is not installed on the device` even though `mobile: installApp` returned successfully 200–500 ms prior. This is a race condition between the Appium command response and the iOS Springboard registration process.

WHY: When `mobile: installApp` calls `xcrun simctl install`, the installation is performed by `SimulatorBridge.installApplication()` in the `CoreSimulator` framework, which copies the `.app` bundle to the simulator's data container and then sends an XPC notification to Springboard to register the bundle identifier. `xcrun simctl install` returns exit code 0 when the file copy completes — not when Springboard's registration callback fires. On simulators under CPU load (e.g., during CI where other test workers are active), Springboard's XPC handler can be delayed by 300–800 ms. If Appium sends the `activateApp` command before Springboard's registry update, `MobileInstallationLookup` returns `NULL` for the bundle ID, causing the "not installed" error. Fix: use `browser.waitUntil(async () => { const state = await driver.queryAppState('com.example.app'); return state >= 4; }, { timeout: 10000, interval: 500 })` after install to poll for `AppState.RUNNING_IN_BACKGROUND` or `RUNNING_IN_FOREGROUND` before calling `activateApp`.

---

**Gotcha C54-5: WDIO v9 `expect(el).toHaveText()` matcher fails against React Native `Text` components that include nested `Text` spans with different styles because `getText()` concatenates all span text without whitespace, collapsing styled sub-strings**
A React Native `<Text>` component with nested inline `<Text>` spans (e.g., `<Text>Price: <Text style={styles.bold}>$9.99</Text></Text>`) returns `"Price: $9.99"` via XCUITest's `accessibilityLabel` (correct), but UIAutomator2's `getText()` method returns `"Price:$9.99"` (no space before the nested span) because UIAutomator2 reads from `View.getContentDescription()` which trims inter-element whitespace during `SpannableString` flattening.

WHY: React Native's Android renderer (Fabric and legacy) maps `<Text>` components to Android's `TextView` with a `SpannableString` content where each nested `<Text>` span is a separate `ReplacementSpan` or `StyleSpan`. When UIAutomator2 calls `node.getText()` on the parent `AccessibilityNodeInfo`, Android's accessibility framework calls `TextView.getText()` which returns the raw `SpannableString`. The framework's `SpannableString.toString()` flattens spans by character positions — if the React Native Fabric renderer emits adjacent spans with no intervening non-styled character (a space character in a plain `<Text>` between spans), the spans are adjacent at the character boundary with no whitespace char between them. UIAutomator2 reads this raw string, producing collapsed text. XCUITest reads from `accessibilityLabel` which React Native populates by traversing its component tree and inserting a space between nested `Text` children, producing the spaced version. Fix: use `expect(el).toHaveText(expect.stringContaining('$9.99'))` or assert on `accessibilityLabel` via `getAttribute('content-desc')` (Android) which reads the accessibility description rather than the raw text content.

## Cycle 55 — 2026-05-14

### New Patterns

**Pattern 568: XCUITest `mobile: swipe` with `velocity` Parameter for Momentum-Sensitive Scroll Tests** [official]
iOS list views behave differently under fast vs. slow flings — fast swipes trigger momentum scrolling that overshoots the target, while slow swipes stop exactly where the gesture ends. XCUITest exposes a `velocity` parameter on `mobile: swipe` (Appium XCUITest driver ≥ 5.3) that maps directly to `XCUIGestureVelocity`, allowing tests to verify that momentum scrolling engages the deceleration physics and that `UIScrollView.decelerationRate` is respected.
```typescript
import { browser } from '@wdio/globals';

async function swipeWithVelocity(
  direction: 'up' | 'down' | 'left' | 'right',
  velocity: number,
  elementId?: string
): Promise<void> {
  const args: Record<string, unknown> = { direction, velocity };
  if (elementId) args.elementId = elementId;
  await browser.execute('mobile: swipe', args);
}

it('fast fling triggers momentum deceleration past midpoint', async () => {
  const list = await $('~productList');
  const beforeScroll = await list.getAttribute('value'); // VoiceOver scroll position

  // fast fling — velocity 3000 pt/s engages UIScrollView momentum physics
  await swipeWithVelocity('up', 3000, await list.elementId);

  await browser.pause(600); // wait for momentum deceleration
  const afterFast = await list.getAttribute('value');
  expect(afterFast).not.toEqual(beforeScroll);

  // slow drag — velocity 200 pt/s, no momentum, precise stop
  await swipeWithVelocity('up', 200, await list.elementId);
  const afterSlow = await list.getAttribute('value');
  expect(afterSlow).not.toEqual(afterFast); // scrolled more, but proportionally less
});
```
Tradeoff: The `velocity` parameter was added in XCUITest driver 5.3 and is silently ignored in earlier versions — the swipe executes at a default velocity with no error. On physical devices running iOS 17+, velocities above ~3500 pt/s are clamped by `XCUIGestureVelocity` to its maximum value. In CI simulators, momentum animations are often disabled via `UIView.setAnimationsEnabled(false)` in the test host, making velocity-based scroll assertions unreliable unless animations are explicitly re-enabled with `mobile: setSimulatorMetricsOverride` before the test.

**Pattern 569: UIAutomator2 `mobile: scroll` with `strategy` and `selector` for Element-Targeted Scrollable Container Navigation** [official]
UIAutomator2's `mobile: scroll` command accepts a `strategy` field (`"accessibility id"`, `"id"`, `"class name"`, `"-android uiautomator"`) that specifies how the `selector` argument is interpreted to identify the target element to scroll to within a scrollable container. This replaces the fragile `scrollTo` pattern that relied on `UiScrollable.scrollTextIntoView()` and is compatible with `RecyclerView`, `NestedScrollView`, and `ListView` containers.
```typescript
import { browser } from '@wdio/globals';

async function scrollToElement(
  scrollableId: string,
  targetAccessibilityId: string
): Promise<WebdriverIO.Element> {
  await browser.execute('mobile: scroll', {
    elementId: (await $(`~${scrollableId}`)).elementId,
    strategy: 'accessibility id',
    selector: targetAccessibilityId,
  });
  const el = await $(`~${targetAccessibilityId}`);
  await el.waitForDisplayed({ timeout: 5000 });
  return el;
}

it('scrolls RecyclerView to target item and verifies visibility', async () => {
  await browser.startActivity('com.example', '.MainActivity');
  const target = await scrollToElement('productList', 'product-item-42');
  await expect(target).toBeDisplayed();

  const text = await target.$('~productTitle').getText();
  expect(text).toBe('Product #42');
});
```
Tradeoff: `mobile: scroll` with `strategy`/`selector` performs a `UiScrollable.scrollIntoView()` under the hood, which scrolls only within the **first** scrollable ancestor of the identified scrollable container. Nested scrollable containers (e.g., a horizontal `RecyclerView` inside a vertical `NestedScrollView`) will scroll the outer container, not the inner one — pass the `elementId` of the inner container explicitly in that case. The command also fails with `ScrollableNotFoundException` if the container has `android:focusable="false"` set on its root view — work around this with `mobile: swipe` in that scenario.

**Pattern 570: WDIO v9 `browser.action('pointer')` W3C Actions API for Complex Multi-Touch Gesture Composition on iOS and Android** [official]
The W3C Actions API (`browser.action('pointer')`) provides a low-level, cross-platform interface for composing multi-step pointer sequences including pinch, rotate, and two-finger drag. Unlike high-level Appium commands (`mobile: pinch`, `mobile: rotate`), the Actions API exposes the raw pointer timeline, allowing precise control over finger placement, movement interpolation, and timing between touch events.
```typescript
import { browser } from '@wdio/globals';

async function pinchOpen(
  el: WebdriverIO.Element,
  scalePercent: number = 150,
  durationMs: number = 800
): Promise<void> {
  const rect = await el.getElementRect(el.elementId);
  const cx = rect.x + rect.width / 2;
  const cy = rect.y + rect.height / 2;
  const offset = (rect.width / 4) * (scalePercent / 100);

  const f1 = browser.action('pointer', { parameters: { pointerType: 'touch' } });
  const f2 = browser.action('pointer', { parameters: { pointerType: 'touch' } });

  f1.move({ x: cx - 20, y: cy, duration: 0 }).down().pause(100)
    .move({ x: cx - offset, y: cy, duration: durationMs }).up();
  f2.move({ x: cx + 20, y: cy, duration: 0 }).down().pause(100)
    .move({ x: cx + offset, y: cy, duration: durationMs }).up();

  await browser.actions([f1, f2]);
}

it('pinch-open expands photo viewer to full screen', async () => {
  const photo = await $('~photoViewer');
  await pinchOpen(photo, 200, 600);
  await browser.pause(400);
  const fullscreen = await $('~fullscreenPhotoViewer');
  await expect(fullscreen).toBeDisplayed();
});
```
Tradeoff: The W3C Actions API is supported by both XCUITest (via Appium's `xcuitest-driver` WDIO implementation) and UIAutomator2, but coordinate systems differ: iOS uses logical points while Android uses density-independent pixels (dp) at the current display density. `getElementRect()` returns values in the respective device's coordinate space, so the calculation above is portable. However, Android emulators running on ARM Macs via Rosetta may add 15–30 ms of jitter per action tick, making fast gesture sequences (< 200 ms total) unreliable — use `durationMs >= 400` for emulator-compatible tests.

**Pattern 571: Appium 2 `mobile: getContexts` with `returnDetailedContexts: true` for Reliable WebView Attachment by URL Pattern** [official]
Appium 2 with UIAutomator2 3.x introduced the `returnDetailedContexts` option on `mobile: getContexts`, which returns an array of context objects each containing `id`, `title`, `url`, and `packageName`. This enables matching the correct WebView context by URL pattern rather than by positional index, which is brittle when multiple WebViews are present (e.g., an in-app browser alongside the main content WebView).
```typescript
import { browser } from '@wdio/globals';

interface DetailedContext {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  url: string;
  packageName?: string;
}

async function switchToWebViewByUrl(urlPattern: RegExp): Promise<string> {
  const contexts = await browser.execute('mobile: getContexts', {
    returnDetailedContexts: true,
  }) as DetailedContext[];

  const target = contexts.find(
    (ctx) => ctx.id !== 'NATIVE_APP' && urlPattern.test(ctx.url)
  );

  if (!target) {
    const available = contexts.map((c) => `${c.id}:${c.url}`).join(', ');
    throw new Error(`No WebView matching ${urlPattern}. Available: ${available}`);
  }

  await browser.switchContext(target.id);
  return target.id;
}

it('switches to checkout webview and verifies form fields', async () => {
  await $('~checkoutButton').click();
  const ctx = await switchToWebViewByUrl(/checkout\.example\.com/);
  expect(ctx).toMatch(/^WEBVIEW/);

  const emailField = await $('input[name="email"]');
  await emailField.setValue('test@example.com');
  await expect(emailField).toHaveValue('test@example.com');
  await browser.switchContext('NATIVE_APP');
});
```
Tradeoff: `returnDetailedContexts: true` requires Chrome DevTools Protocol to be enabled in the WebView, which means `WebView.setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled(true)` must be called in the app under test. Production apps commonly disable this for security; coordinate with the mobile team to enable it via a build flag in test builds. On Android API < 27 (Android 8), `packageName` is not populated in the context object — use `url` or `title` for matching only. Also, context metadata is populated asynchronously after the WebView loads; use `browser.waitUntil()` to poll `getContexts` until the target URL is present before switching.

**Pattern 572: XCUITest `mobile: tap` with `x`/`y` Absolute Coordinates for Tapping Non-Accessible Map Pin Elements** [official]
Map and canvas elements rendered via `MKMapView` or `GLKView` do not expose individual pin or marker elements through the XCUITest accessibility tree — the entire map is a single accessibility element. To tap specific map pins, `mobile: tap` with absolute screen coordinates (derived from the expected pin location in the app's coordinate-space-to-screen-coordinate projection) is the only reliable automation approach.
```typescript
import { browser } from '@wdio/globals';

interface ScreenCoordinate { x: number; y: number }

async function tapMapCoordinate(coord: ScreenCoordinate): Promise<void> {
  await browser.execute('mobile: tap', { x: coord.x, y: coord.y });
}

async function getExpectedPinScreenPosition(
  latitude: number,
  longitude: number
): Promise<ScreenCoordinate> {
  // App exposes a JS bridge to convert geo coords to screen coords
  return browser.execute(
    `return window.mapBridge.geoToScreen(${latitude}, ${longitude})`
  ) as Promise<ScreenCoordinate>;
}

it('taps a map pin and shows the info panel', async () => {
  await $('~mapView').waitForDisplayed({ timeout: 5000 });
  await browser.pause(1000); // wait for map tiles to render

  const pinCoord = await getExpectedPinScreenPosition(37.7749, -122.4194);
  await tapMapCoordinate(pinCoord);

  const infoPanel = await $('~pinInfoPanel');
  await infoPanel.waitForDisplayed({ timeout: 3000 });
  await expect(infoPanel.$('~pinTitle')).toHaveText('San Francisco');
});
```
Tradeoff: Absolute coordinate tapping is fundamentally brittle across device sizes and orientations because the screen-space projection of a geo-coordinate depends on the map's visible region, zoom level, and device pixel density. This pattern only works reliably if the app exposes a coordinate conversion bridge (JS or native) or if the test resets the map to a known pan/zoom state before each tap assertion. On devices with Display Zoom enabled, coordinates returned by the coordinate bridge must be divided by the zoom scale factor to get correct physical screen coordinates — check `mobile: activeAppInfo` for the current display scale.

**Pattern 573: WDIO v9 `browser.savePDF()` via CDP for Capturing WebView Content as PDF in Regression Baselines** [official]
WebdriverIO v9 exposes `browser.savePDF()` which triggers a CDP `Page.printToPDF` call in the current WebView context. This is useful for capturing the rendered state of document-heavy pages (invoices, reports, terms screens) as a regression baseline artifact rather than relying on pixel-diff screenshots that break when fonts or antialiasing differ across simulators.
```typescript
import { browser } from '@wdio/globals';
import * as fs from 'fs';
import * as path from 'path';

async function captureWebViewAsPdf(
  outputDir: string,
  filename: string
): Promise<string> {
  const outPath = path.join(outputDir, filename);
  await browser.savePDF(outPath, {
    orientation: 'Portrait',
    background: true,
    width: 21,
    height: 29.7,
    top: 0, bottom: 0, left: 0, right: 0,
    shrinkToFit: true,
    pageRanges: [],
  });
  return outPath;
}

it('invoice screen renders all required fields', async () => {
  await $('~viewInvoiceButton').click();
  await browser.switchContext('WEBVIEW_com.example.app');
  await browser.waitUntil(
    async () => (await browser.getUrl()).includes('/invoice'),
    { timeout: 5000 }
  );

  const pdfPath = await captureWebViewAsPdf('./artifacts', 'invoice-test.pdf');
  expect(fs.existsSync(pdfPath)).toBe(true);
  const stat = fs.statSync(pdfPath);
  expect(stat.size).toBeGreaterThan(5000); // non-trivial PDF rendered

  await browser.switchContext('NATIVE_APP');
});
```
Tradeoff: `browser.savePDF()` is only available when the active context is a WebView with CDP enabled — calling it from `NATIVE_APP` context throws `unknown command: savePDF`. PDF generation via CDP `Page.printToPDF` renders the page at a fixed 96 DPI without accounting for the device pixel ratio, so the PDF will appear lower-resolution than a screenshot captured with `browser.saveScreenshot()`. For visual regression, use specialized PDF diff tools (e.g., `pdf-visual-diff` npm package) rather than byte-for-byte file comparison, as PDF rendering introduces minor floating-point variation in path coordinates.

**Pattern 574: Appium 2 `mobile: deepLink` for Testing Universal Link Disambiguation Sheet on iOS** [official]
On iOS 16+, tapping a universal link that maps to an installed app presents a system disambiguation sheet asking the user whether to open in Safari or in the app. `mobile: deepLink` (XCUITest driver) bypasses this sheet by invoking `xcrun simctl openurl` directly against the simulator, opening the app via the registered Universal Link handler without triggering the disambiguation UI. For real-device flows where the disambiguation sheet must be tested, `mobile: deepLink` with `presentingApp: 'com.apple.MobileSafari'` forces the sheet to appear.
```typescript
import { browser, $ } from '@wdio/globals';

async function openViaDeepLink(url: string, expectApp: string): Promise<void> {
  await browser.execute('mobile: deepLink', {
    url,
    package: expectApp, // iOS: bundleId; Android: package name
  });
}

it('universal link opens app at correct route without disambiguation', async () => {
  // Simulate cold-start from Safari deep link
  await browser.execute('mobile: terminateApp', { bundleId: 'com.example.app' });
  await browser.pause(500);

  await openViaDeepLink('https://www.example.com/products/42', 'com.example.app');

  // App should launch directly to product detail without disambiguation
  const productTitle = await $('~productDetailTitle');
  await productTitle.waitForDisplayed({ timeout: 6000 });
  await expect(productTitle).toHaveText('Product #42');
});

it('deepLink via Safari triggers disambiguation sheet', async () => {
  await browser.execute('mobile: deepLink', {
    url: 'https://www.example.com/products/42',
    package: 'com.example.app',
    presentingApp: 'com.apple.MobileSafari',
  });

  const openButton = await $('~Open'); // system sheet "Open" button
  await openButton.waitForDisplayed({ timeout: 4000 });
  await expect(openButton).toBeDisplayed();
});
```
Tradeoff: `mobile: deepLink` on iOS only works on simulators for the non-Safari variant (the `xcrun simctl openurl` path). On physical iOS devices, the command falls back to `idb_companion`'s `open_url` which has the same disambiguation-bypass behavior but requires `idb_companion` to be installed and paired. The `presentingApp` option is iOS-only and requires XCUITest driver ≥ 7.1. On Android, `mobile: deepLink` invokes `adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d <url>` which bypasses the chooser dialog entirely — there is no Android equivalent for forcing the disambiguation dialog in automation.

**Pattern 575: UIAutomator2 `mobile: pressKey` with `keycode` for Android Back Navigation Including Edge-to-Edge Gesture Interference** [official]
Android 13+ apps built targeting SDK 33 with `android:enableOnBackInvokedCallback="true"` use the new Predictive Back API, which intercepts the system back gesture before it reaches the activity's `onBackPressed()`. UIAutomator2's `mobile: pressKey` with `keycode: 4` (KEYCODE_BACK) directly injects a `KeyEvent.KEYCODE_BACK` via the `InputManager`, bypassing the gesture recognizer entirely. This makes it the only reliable way to trigger back navigation in tests regardless of whether the app uses the legacy or predictive back API.
```typescript
import { browser } from '@wdio/globals';

async function pressBack(): Promise<void> {
  await browser.execute('mobile: pressKey', { keycode: 4 });
}

async function pressHome(): Promise<void> {
  await browser.execute('mobile: pressKey', { keycode: 3 });
}

it('back from product detail returns to product list', async () => {
  await browser.startActivity('com.example', '.ProductDetailActivity');
  const title = await $('~productDetailTitle');
  await title.waitForDisplayed({ timeout: 5000 });
  await expect(title).toBeDisplayed();

  await pressBack();

  const list = await $('~productListContainer');
  await list.waitForDisplayed({ timeout: 4000 });
  await expect(list).toBeDisplayed();
});

it('back gesture does not trigger on swipe-back-intercepting view pager', async () => {
  await $('~swipeGallery').waitForDisplayed({ timeout: 5000 });
  // Swipe back gesture consumed by ViewPager — pressKey bypasses it
  await pressBack();
  await expect($('~homeScreen')).toBeDisplayed({ timeout: 3000 });
});
```
Tradeoff: `mobile: pressKey` with KEYCODE_BACK (4) fires a `KeyEvent.ACTION_DOWN` followed by `KeyEvent.ACTION_UP` synchronously via `UiDevice.pressBack()`, which is not intercepted by the gesture navigation bar. Apps that implement a `OnBackPressedCallback` registered with `requireActivity().onBackPressedDispatcher` (Jetpack back-press handling) will correctly receive this event. The issue arises only when apps use `dispatchKeyEvent` overrides that swallow `KEYCODE_BACK` for custom dismiss animations — in those cases, use `mobile: swipe` from the left edge (`x: 5, y: 400, endX: 200, endY: 400`) to trigger the gesture recognizer path instead.

**Pattern 576: WDIO v9 `element.scrollIntoView()` for Cross-Platform Scroll-Until-Visible with Automatic Platform Detection** [official]
WebdriverIO v9 introduced a cross-platform `element.scrollIntoView()` implementation that delegates to `mobile: scroll` on native contexts and to a JavaScript `scrollIntoView()` call on WebView contexts, detecting the current context automatically. This eliminates platform-specific branching in page objects and is more reliable than custom scroll loops because it uses the driver's built-in element visibility check rather than polling `isDisplayed()`.
```typescript
import { $ } from '@wdio/globals';

class ProductListPage {
  private get list() { return $('~productList'); }
  private itemSelector(id: string) { return $(`~product-item-${id}`); }

  async scrollToItem(id: string): Promise<WebdriverIO.Element> {
    const item = this.itemSelector(id);
    // Works in NATIVE_APP (UIAutomator2/XCUITest) and WEBVIEW contexts
    await item.scrollIntoView();
    await item.waitForDisplayed({ timeout: 4000 });
    return item;
  }

  async verifyItemVisible(id: string, expectedTitle: string): Promise<void> {
    const item = await this.scrollToItem(id);
    await expect(item.$('~itemTitle')).toHaveText(expectedTitle);
  }
}

it('scrolls product list and verifies item title', async () => {
  const page = new ProductListPage();
  await page.verifyItemVisible('product-99', 'Widget Pro Max');
});
```
Tradeoff: `element.scrollIntoView()` on native Android uses a `UiScrollable.scrollIntoView()` predicate search internally, which only works if the target element's accessibility ID is known to the `RecyclerView` adapter before rendering (i.e., the element must be virtualized, not just off-screen). Elements that are not yet rendered in the `RecyclerView`'s view pool will not be found and the command throws `NoSuchElementException`. In that case, fall back to `mobile: scroll` with `strategy: "-android uiautomator"` and a UiSelector expression. On iOS, `scrollIntoView()` triggers `XCUIElement.scrollToVisible()` which scrolls the element's closest scrollable ancestor, not the root scroll view — this can be unexpected when multiple nested scroll views are present.

**Pattern 577: Appium 2 `mobile: getDeviceInfo` for Runtime Device Capability Gating in Cross-Device Test Suites** [official]
`mobile: getDeviceInfo` (available in XCUITest driver ≥ 5.0 and UIAutomator2 ≥ 3.0) returns a structured object containing OS version, device model, screen dimensions, locale, and hardware feature flags. Reading this at test startup allows tests to gate capabilities (NFC, biometrics, folded screen) without hardcoding device names in test code, making suites portable across device farms.
```typescript
import { browser } from '@wdio/globals';

interface DeviceInfo {
  platformName: string;
  platformVersion: string;
  deviceName: string;
  screenSize: { width: number; height: number };
  locale: string;
  isSimulator: boolean;
}

let deviceInfo: DeviceInfo;

before(async () => {
  deviceInfo = await browser.execute('mobile: getDeviceInfo') as DeviceInfo;
  console.log(`Running on: ${deviceInfo.deviceName} iOS ${deviceInfo.platformVersion}`);
});

async function skipIfSimulator(testFn: () => Promise<void>): Promise<void> {
  if (deviceInfo?.isSimulator) {
    console.warn('Skipping: real device only test');
    return;
  }
  await testFn();
}

it('biometric auth works on real device', async () => {
  await skipIfSimulator(async () => {
    await $('~loginWithFaceId').click();
    await browser.execute('mobile: enrollBiometric', { isEnabled: true });
    await browser.execute('mobile: sendBiometricMatch', { type: 'faceId', match: true });
    await expect($('~homeScreen')).toBeDisplayed({ timeout: 5000 });
  });
});
```
Tradeoff: `mobile: getDeviceInfo` on Android returns different field names than on iOS — `platformVersion` is a string on iOS but can be a string like `"13"` or `"13.0"` on Android depending on the UIAutomator2 version. Normalize by parsing with `parseFloat()` for version comparisons. The `isSimulator` field is iOS-only; on Android use `deviceInfo.deviceName.toLowerCase().includes('emulator')` or check `adb shell getprop ro.kernel.qemu`. Calling `getDeviceInfo` in `before()` adds ~200–400 ms to suite startup — acceptable for most suites but worth caching at the module level if called from multiple `describe` blocks.

**Pattern 578: WDIO v9 `browser.waitUntil()` with Exponential Backoff for Flake-Resistant App State Polling** [community]
The default `browser.waitUntil()` uses a fixed polling interval (`interval` option, default 500 ms). In tests that poll for transient app states (loading indicators, async state transitions, network-dependent UI), fixed-interval polling either over-polls (wasting resources in fast environments) or under-polls (missing brief states in slow environments). A custom exponential backoff wrapper increases polling frequency early and backs off as the wait extends, balancing responsiveness and CPU load.
```typescript
import { browser } from '@wdio/globals';

async function waitUntilExponential<T>(
  condition: () => Promise<T | false>,
  opts: { timeout: number; initialInterval?: number; maxInterval?: number; label?: string }
): Promise<T> {
  const { timeout, initialInterval = 100, maxInterval = 2000, label = 'condition' } = opts;
  let interval = initialInterval;
  const deadline = Date.now() + timeout;

  while (Date.now() < deadline) {
    const result = await condition();
    if (result !== false) return result as T;
    await browser.pause(Math.min(interval, deadline - Date.now(), maxInterval));
    interval = Math.min(interval * 2, maxInterval);
  }

  throw new Error(`Timed out after ${timeout}ms waiting for: ${label}`);
}

it('waits for sync indicator to disappear with exponential backoff', async () => {
  await $('~syncButton').click();

  await waitUntilExponential(
    async () => {
      const spinner = await $('~syncSpinner');
      return !(await spinner.isDisplayed()) || spinner;
    },
    { timeout: 15000, initialInterval: 100, maxInterval: 1000, label: 'sync completion' }
  );

  await expect($('~syncCompleteIcon')).toBeDisplayed();
});
```
Tradeoff: This pattern replaces WDIO's built-in `waitUntil` polling contract with a custom loop, losing the automatic `TimeoutError` message formatting that WDIO generates (which includes the last driver state). The custom implementation catches `NoSuchElementException` from `$()` calls implicitly only if the condition function itself catches them — wrap the `condition` body in a try/catch if the element may not exist. Also, exponential backoff with `initialInterval: 100` means up to 10 fast polls in the first second, which can load a CI device's Appium server with rapid HTTP round-trips; set `initialInterval: 200` for device farm runs.

---

**Pattern 579: XCUITest `mobile: source` with `format: 'description'` for Fast Structural Assertions Without Full XML Parse** [official]
`driver.source()` (equivalent to `mobile: source` with default JSON format) fetches the entire accessibility tree as a JSON/XML blob — on complex screens this can return 500 KB–2 MB payloads that take 800–2000 ms to transfer and parse. For structural assertions (e.g., "does the screen contain a modal?"), `mobile: source` with `format: 'description'` returns a compact human-readable string representation of the accessibility tree that is 5–10x smaller and transferred in 100–300 ms.
```typescript
import { browser } from '@wdio/globals';

async function pageSourceDescription(): Promise<string> {
  const desc = await browser.execute('mobile: source', { format: 'description' });
  return String(desc);
}

async function assertModalPresent(modalAccessibilityId: string): Promise<void> {
  const description = await pageSourceDescription();
  if (!description.includes(modalAccessibilityId)) {
    throw new Error(
      `Expected modal '${modalAccessibilityId}' not found in page description.\n` +
      `Description excerpt: ${description.slice(0, 500)}`
    );
  }
}

it('error modal is shown after failed purchase', async () => {
  await $('~buyButton').click();
  await $('~confirmPurchaseButton').click();

  // Fast structural check before interacting with modal elements
  await browser.waitUntil(
    async () => {
      const src = await pageSourceDescription();
      return src.includes('purchaseErrorModal');
    },
    { timeout: 8000, interval: 400 }
  );

  await assertModalPresent('purchaseErrorModal');
  await expect($('~errorTitle')).toHaveText('Payment Failed');
});
```
Tradeoff: The `description` format is XCUITest-only — UIAutomator2 does not support `format: 'description'` and will throw `unknown argument: format`. For cross-platform tests, add a platform guard: use `description` format on iOS and fall back to substring search on the XML string from `driver.source()` on Android. The description format is a human-readable string, not a machine-parseable structure — use only for presence/absence assertions (`includes()`). Avoid parsing positions, attributes, or counts from the description string, as those patterns are fragile against Apple changing the description format.

---

**Pattern 580: Appium 2 `mobile: launchApp` with `arguments` Array for Feature-Flag-Gated Test State Initialization** [official]
Both XCUITest and UIAutomator2 support passing launch arguments via capabilities or `mobile: launchApp`'s `arguments` array. iOS apps read these via `ProcessInfo.processInfo.arguments` and Android apps read them via `Intent.getStringExtra()`. Using launch arguments instead of in-test setup flows (tapping through onboarding, filling in credentials) reduces test setup time by 60–80% and eliminates UI-layer flakiness in the setup path.
```typescript
import { browser } from '@wdio/globals';

const LAUNCH_ARGS = {
  skipOnboarding: '-SKIP_ONBOARDING',
  mockAuth: '-MOCK_AUTH',
  featureFlag: (flag: string, enabled: boolean) =>
    `-FF_${flag.toUpperCase()}=${enabled ? '1' : '0'}`,
};

async function relaunchWithFlags(...args: string[]): Promise<void> {
  await browser.execute('mobile: terminateApp', { bundleId: 'com.example.app' });
  await browser.execute('mobile: launchApp', {
    bundleId: 'com.example.app',
    arguments: args,
  });
}

it('new checkout flow is shown when feature flag enabled', async () => {
  await relaunchWithFlags(
    LAUNCH_ARGS.skipOnboarding,
    LAUNCH_ARGS.mockAuth,
    LAUNCH_ARGS.featureFlag('NEW_CHECKOUT', true)
  );

  await $('~homeScreen').waitForDisplayed({ timeout: 6000 });
  await $('~cartButton').click();

  const newCheckout = await $('~newCheckoutFlowContainer');
  await expect(newCheckout).toBeDisplayed();
});
```
Tradeoff: Launch arguments on iOS are only accessible via `ProcessInfo.arguments` — they are not accessible via `UserDefaults`, `NSUserActivity`, or other mechanisms. Apps that read feature flags from a remote config service must have a local override mechanism that checks `ProcessInfo.arguments` first. On Android, `mobile: launchApp` with `arguments` passes them as `Intent` extras — the app must explicitly read each key via `intent.getStringExtra(key)`. There is no standard convention for launch argument names across iOS and Android, so maintain a shared constants file for argument key names to keep iOS (dash-prefixed) and Android (plain string) keys aligned.

---

**Pattern 581: WDIO v9 `browser.uploadFile()` for Testing File Picker Interactions in Hybrid Apps** [official]
WDIO v9 provides `browser.uploadFile(localPath)` which, in a WebView context, uploads a local file via ChromeDriver's `Input.setFiles` CDP command. This allows tests to programmatically fulfill `<input type="file">` interactions without triggering the native file picker system sheet (which is not automatable on iOS and requires `mobile: openFile` workarounds on Android).
```typescript
import { browser, $ } from '@wdio/globals';
import * as path from 'path';
import * as fs from 'fs';

async function uploadTestFile(
  inputSelector: string,
  filename: string,
  content: string
): Promise<void> {
  // Write temp file
  const tmpPath = path.join(process.cwd(), 'tmp', filename);
  fs.mkdirSync(path.dirname(tmpPath), { recursive: true });
  fs.writeFileSync(tmpPath, content);

  // Switch to WebView and upload
  await browser.switchContext('WEBVIEW_com.example.app');
  const remotePath = await browser.uploadFile(tmpPath);
  const fileInput = await $(inputSelector);
  await fileInput.addValue(remotePath);

  // Verify upload triggered
  await expect($(inputSelector)).toHaveAttribute('data-file-selected', 'true');
  await browser.switchContext('NATIVE_APP');
}

it('CSV import flow processes uploaded file correctly', async () => {
  await $('~importButton').click();
  await uploadTestFile(
    'input[data-testid="csvUpload"]',
    'test-import.csv',
    'id,name,price\n1,Widget,9.99\n2,Gadget,19.99'
  );

  const successBanner = await $('[data-testid="importSuccess"]');
  await successBanner.waitForDisplayed({ timeout: 8000 });
  await expect(successBanner).toHaveText('2 products imported');
});
```
Tradeoff: `browser.uploadFile()` with `Input.setFiles` only works in WebView contexts where ChromeDriver controls the page — it has no effect in the native app context. On iOS, the file is uploaded from the Mac/CI runner's filesystem to the simulator via a temporary path managed by the `WebDriverAgent` file transfer API; on real iOS devices, this file transfer goes through the `idb_companion` tunnel and can be 2–5x slower for files > 1 MB. The `<input type="file">` must not be `display: none` or have `visibility: hidden` for `addValue()` to succeed — use JavaScript to temporarily make it visible if the app hides it for custom styling.

---

**Pattern 582: Appium 2 `mobile: alert` for Handling System Permission Dialogs and Custom Alert Actions** [official]
iOS system permission dialogs (location, camera, notifications, contacts) are rendered outside the app's accessibility tree by Springboard and cannot be located via standard `$()` element queries. `mobile: alert` provides `getText`, `accept`, `dismiss`, and `sendKeys` actions that directly interact with the frontmost system alert, regardless of whether it is a Springboard permission dialog or an app-level `UIAlertController`.
```typescript
import { browser } from '@wdio/globals';

type AlertAction = 'accept' | 'dismiss' | 'getText';

async function handleSystemAlert(
  action: AlertAction,
  buttonLabel?: string
): Promise<string | void> {
  try {
    if (action === 'getText') {
      return String(await browser.execute('mobile: alert', { action: 'getText' }));
    }
    await browser.execute('mobile: alert', {
      action,
      ...(buttonLabel ? { buttonLabel } : {}),
    });
  } catch {
    // No alert present — not an error in most flows
  }
}

async function grantPermissionIfPrompted(permissionText: RegExp): Promise<boolean> {
  await browser.pause(500); // system alerts appear asynchronously
  const alertText = await handleSystemAlert('getText');
  if (alertText && permissionText.test(alertText)) {
    await handleSystemAlert('accept', 'Allow While Using App');
    return true;
  }
  return false;
}

it('location permission prompt is accepted and map loads', async () => {
  await $('~findNearbyButton').click();
  const granted = await grantPermissionIfPrompted(/location/i);
  expect(granted).toBe(true);

  await $('~nearbyResultsList').waitForDisplayed({ timeout: 8000 });
  await expect($('~nearbyResultsList')).toBeDisplayed();
});
```
Tradeoff: `mobile: alert` with `action: 'accept'` clicks the **first positive button** (rightmost button in a standard iOS alert). If the permission dialog has multiple allow options ("Allow Once" vs "Allow While Using App" vs "Don't Allow"), specify `buttonLabel` explicitly to avoid non-deterministically clicking the wrong option. On iOS 17+, some system alerts (Screen Time, App Privacy Report) are presented as `UIHostingController` SwiftUI views rather than `UIAlertController` — these are not intercepted by `mobile: alert` and require XCUITest coordinate-based taps on known button positions. Test this in your specific iOS version matrix before relying on `mobile: alert` for all permission handling.

### Community Gotchas

**Gotcha C55-1: WDIO v9 `element.click()` on Android `FloatingActionButton` triggers the button's ripple animation touch feedback but the click event is not delivered when `elevation` > 8dp and another view's shadow overlaps the touch target**
On Android 12+ with Material You, `FloatingActionButton` elements with `elevation` > 8dp cast a hardware-accelerated shadow rendered by `RenderThread`. When a `BottomSheet` or `CardView` with a matching or higher `elevation` is partially overlaid on the FAB's touch target (even by 1 px), Android's touch dispatching routes the `MotionEvent` to the shadow-casting view's `TouchDelegate` area rather than to the FAB itself. UIAutomator2 resolves the element's bounds correctly and sends the `ACTION_DOWN`/`ACTION_UP` to the center of those bounds, but the `InputEventReceiver` on the overlapping view consumes the event. The test receives no error — the ripple plays, the button appears clicked, but the `onClick` listener is never called.

WHY: Android's view touch dispatching calls `ViewGroup.onInterceptTouchEvent()` up the hierarchy from the root. `MaterialShapeDrawable.onTouchEvent()` (the backing drawable for `CardView` and `BottomSheet`) overrides `onTouchEvent` to return `true` for any touch within its shadow region (padding + elevation-based shadow inset), consuming the event before it reaches the FAB's `OnClickListener`. UIAutomator2 uses `UiObject2.click()` which calls `InputManager.injectMotionEvent()` at the element's center coordinates — the coordinates are correct, but the event is consumed by the overlapping shadow region. Fix: use `browser.execute('mobile: shell', { command: 'input', args: ['tap', String(x), String(y)] })` with coordinates offset to a non-overlapping area of the FAB, or use `await driver.execute('mobile: scroll', ...)` to scroll the overlapping element out of the FAB's shadow zone before clicking.

---

**Gotcha C55-2: XCUITest `element.clearValue()` on a `UITextField` with a `RightView` accessory (search clear button) leaves a zero-width space character in the field on iOS 16.4–17.2**
After calling `element.clearValue()` on a `UITextField` that has an `inputAccessoryView` or a `rightView` configured (common in search fields), the field appears visually empty and `element.getText()` returns an empty string, but `element.getValue()` returns a zero-width space character (Unicode U+200B). Subsequent `element.setValue('newText')` calls prepend to the zero-width space, producing the sentinel plus new text as the actual field content. This causes `expect(el).toHaveValue('newText')` to pass (because `expect` uses `getText()` which strips the character) while the server-side API call includes the hidden prefix, resulting in validation errors.

WHY: XCUITest's `XCUIElement.clearText()` implementation (called by `clearValue()` via the Appium bridge) works by calling `element.tap()` to focus, then issuing delete keystrokes for each character. On iOS 16.4+, `UITextField.rightView` accessory buttons intercept the focus `tap()` action and trigger the built-in clear button action, which calls `UITextField.text = ""` directly. However, a concurrent `UITextFieldDelegate.textFieldShouldClear()` implementation in some apps inserts a zero-width space as a placeholder sentinel before the delegate returns `true`, which persists after the clear. XCUITest's subsequent delete sequence then targets the already-empty field (it calculates current length before the accessory clear fires), leaving the sentinel in place. Fix: after `clearValue()`, use `await element.setValue('')` (which does a full replace rather than delete-chars), then verify with `getValue()` rather than `getText()`.

---

**Gotcha C55-3: Appium 2 `driver.getPageSource()` on Android takes 3–8 seconds when the app uses `ViewPager2` with 5+ off-screen pages preloaded via `offscreenPageLimit`**
`ViewPager2` with `setOffscreenPageLimit(5)` maintains 5 pages in memory on each side of the current page. When `driver.getPageSource()` is called, UIAutomator2 dumps the full accessibility tree via `UiAutomation.getRootInActiveWindow()`, which traverses all attached `View` hierarchies including the off-screen pages. Each off-screen page's `RecyclerView` adapter creates accessibility nodes for all bound items, even those not currently visible. On a test app with 5 off-screen pages each containing 50-item `RecyclerView` lists, `getPageSource()` generates an accessibility tree with 500+ extra nodes, taking 3–8 seconds to serialize to XML.

WHY: Android's `AccessibilityNodeInfoDumper.dumpWindowToFile()` (called internally by UIAutomator2's source dump) traverses every `AccessibilityNodeInfo` returned by `UiAutomation.getRootInActiveWindow()`. `ViewPager2` builds an `AccessibilityNodeProvider` for each off-screen page that it keeps in memory, and Android's accessibility framework includes all visible `AccessibilityNodeProvider` subtrees in the root window's tree, even for views that are not on screen. `RecyclerView`'s `RecyclerViewAccessibilityDelegate` creates `AccessibilityNodeInfo` objects for all currently bound view holders, not just those in the viewport. Fix: use targeted `driver.findElement('accessibility id', 'specificElement')` selectors rather than `getPageSource()` for state assertions, or reset `offscreenPageLimit` to 1 in your test build flavor via a launch argument to eliminate off-screen page bloat during automation runs.

---

**Gotcha C55-4: WDIO v9 `browser.newWindow()` in a WebView context on Android creates a new CDP session that is not automatically associated with the Appium session, causing `browser.switchWindow()` to throw `No window found with title/URL`**
In a hybrid Android app WebView, calling `browser.newWindow('https://example.com')` opens a new tab in the `WebView` (via `WebChromeClient.onCreateWindow()`). The new tab's CDP target is registered with ChromeDriver, but Appium's session state still tracks the original CDP target ID. `browser.switchWindow()` queries ChromeDriver for available targets, finds the new tab, and attempts to switch — but Appium's `switchToWindow` handler maps window handles to its internal context registry, and the new window's handle was never registered in Appium's context registry because `onCreateWindow` fires outside the Appium command pipeline.

WHY: Appium's context management (`switchContext`, `getContexts`) maintains its own registry of context IDs built from `mobile: getContexts` polling calls. When `browser.newWindow()` triggers ChromeDriver's native `window.open()` CDP command, ChromeDriver creates a new tab target (`Target.createTarget`) and registers it in its own target list. Appium's session controller is not notified of this new ChromeDriver target — it only discovers new contexts when `mobile: getContexts` is called explicitly (which triggers Appium's WebView attachment polling). `browser.switchWindow()` in WDIO v9 calls `driver.switchToWindow(handle)` directly against ChromeDriver, bypassing Appium's context registration step. Fix: after `browser.newWindow()`, call `await browser.execute('mobile: getContexts', { returnDetailedContexts: true })` to force Appium to re-enumerate CDP targets and update its registry, then use `browser.switchContext()` with the newly discovered context ID instead of `browser.switchWindow()`.

---

**Gotcha C55-5: UIAutomator2 `element.dragAndDrop()` with a duration < 500 ms on Android 14 (API 34) causes the drop target to receive `DragEvent.ACTION_DRAG_EXITED` before `ACTION_DROP` when the receiving `View` uses `setOnDragListener` with `View.DragFlags.GLOBAL`**
On Android 14, `View.startDragAndDrop()` uses the system's `DragAndDropController` which enforces a minimum gesture duration before the `ACTION_DROP` event is dispatched to the drop target. When UIAutomator2's `element.dragAndDrop()` is called with `duration < 500`, the `InputManager` injects `ACTION_MOVE` events too rapidly for the `DragAndDropController`'s state machine to transition from `DRAGGING` to `DROPPED` state. Instead, the rapid movement triggers the `EXITED` state because the velocity exceeds the `DragAndDropController.MAX_DRAG_VELOCITY` threshold, causing the drop target's `onDragListener` to receive `ACTION_DRAG_EXITED` immediately after `ACTION_DRAG_ENTERED`, and the final `ACTION_UP` does not translate into `ACTION_DROP`.

WHY: Android 14's `DragAndDropController.onInputEvent()` tracks the drag gesture state via an internal finite state machine. When `MotionEvent.ACTION_UP` is received while the FSM is in state `DRAGGING` (not yet `OVER_TARGET`), the controller checks whether the final pointer position is within a registered `DropPermissions` zone. If the drag velocity (calculated from the last two `ACTION_MOVE` events) exceeds `MAX_DRAG_VELOCITY` (~2000 px/s), the FSM transitions to `CANCELLED` instead of `DROPPED`, firing `ACTION_DRAG_EXITED` to all listeners and `ACTION_DRAG_ENDED` with `getResult()` returning `false`. UIAutomator2's `dragAndDrop()` with `duration: 200` generates `ACTION_MOVE` intervals of ~16 ms over 200 ms, producing velocities of ~1875 px/s per frame — just below the threshold on slower emulators but exceeding it on Pixel 8 Pro hardware. Fix: always use `duration >= 600` for drag-and-drop operations on Android 14 devices. Verify behavior with `await driver.execute('mobile: shell', { command: 'dumpsys', args: ['input'] })` to confirm input injection velocity before submitting CI results.

## Cycle 56 — 2026-05-14

### New Patterns

**Pattern 583: WDIO v9 `browser.getContexts()` with `returnDetailedContexts: true` and `returnAndroidDescriptionData: true` for Layout-Aware WebView Context Selection** [official]
When a hybrid Android app renders multiple `WebView` instances embedded in different layout regions (e.g., a bottom-sheet WebView alongside a full-screen product detail WebView), `getContexts()` without detailed options returns opaque string IDs like `WEBVIEW_com.example.app` and `WEBVIEW_com.example.app_2`. The `returnAndroidDescriptionData` flag enriches each context entry with `screenX`, `screenY`, `width`, and `height` fields from UIAutomator2's `View.getLocationOnScreen()`, enabling geometric context selection: choose the WebView whose bounding box intersects the region under test rather than relying on array position or title parsing.
```typescript
import { browser } from '@wdio/globals';

interface DetailedAndroidContext {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  url: string;
  packageName: string;
  webviewPageId: string;
  androidWebviewData?: {
    screenX: number;
    screenY: number;
    width: number;
    height: number;
  };
}

async function switchToWebViewInRegion(
  regionY: number,
  regionHeight: number
): Promise<string> {
  const contexts = await browser.getContexts({
    returnDetailedContexts: true,
    returnAndroidDescriptionData: true,
    androidWebviewConnectTimeout: 8000,
    androidWebviewConnectionRetryTime: 500,
  }) as DetailedAndroidContext[];

  const webviewContexts = contexts.filter(c => c.id !== 'NATIVE_APP');

  const target = webviewContexts.find(ctx => {
    const d = ctx.androidWebviewData;
    if (!d) return false;
    const ctxBottom = d.screenY + d.height;
    const regionBottom = regionY + regionHeight;
    // Overlap check: context region intersects test region
    return d.screenY < regionBottom && ctxBottom > regionY;
  });

  if (!target) {
    throw new Error(
      `No WebView found in region y=${regionY} h=${regionHeight}. ` +
      `Available: ${webviewContexts.map(c => c.id).join(', ')}`
    );
  }

  await browser.switchContext(target.id);
  return target.id;
}

it('bottom-sheet WebView displays correct checkout total', async () => {
  await $('~checkoutButton').click();
  await $('~bottomSheet').waitForDisplayed({ timeout: 5000 });

  const deviceHeight = (await browser.getWindowSize()).height;
  const sheetY = Math.floor(deviceHeight * 0.5);
  const sheetH = Math.floor(deviceHeight * 0.5);

  const ctxId = await switchToWebViewInRegion(sheetY, sheetH);
  expect(ctxId).toContain('WEBVIEW');

  const total = await $('span.checkout-total').getText();
  expect(total).toMatch(/^\$[\d,]+\.\d{2}$/);

  await browser.switchContext('NATIVE_APP');
});
```
Tradeoff: `returnAndroidDescriptionData` triggers an extra UIAutomator2 layout inspection call per context, adding ~80–150 ms overhead per `getContexts()` invocation. On devices with many active WebViews (e.g., a tab-based browser app), this can accumulate. Cache the context ID after the first successful `switchToWebViewInRegion()` call within a test session and only re-query on context loss errors. Also note: `androidWebviewData` is `undefined` for WebViews that are not attached to the window hierarchy at query time (e.g., still loading) — guard with a null-check and retry loop using `browser.waitUntil()`.

---

**Pattern 584: WDIO v9 `browser.swipe()` with `scrollableElement` and `percent` for Carousel Paging Validation Without Hardcoded Coordinates** [official]
Testing a horizontally-paginated carousel requires swiping left/right within the carousel's bounds rather than across the full screen. WDIO v9's `swipe()` accepts a `scrollableElement` reference that constrains the gesture path to the element's bounding box, combined with `percent` (0–1) controlling what fraction of that box is traversed. This eliminates device-width magic numbers and correctly handles carousels embedded in non-full-width containers.
```typescript
import { browser, $ } from '@wdio/globals';

async function swipeCarouselToPage(
  carousel: WebdriverIO.Element,
  targetPage: number,
  currentPage: number
): Promise<void> {
  const delta = targetPage - currentPage;
  const direction = delta > 0 ? 'left' : 'right';
  const steps = Math.abs(delta);

  for (let i = 0; i < steps; i++) {
    await browser.swipe({
      direction,
      duration: 600,
      percent: 0.75,
      scrollableElement: carousel,
    });
    // Allow carousel snap animation to settle
    await browser.pause(350);
  }
}

it('carousel navigates to page 3 and renders correct image', async () => {
  const carousel = await $('~productCarousel');
  await carousel.waitForDisplayed({ timeout: 6000 });

  await swipeCarouselToPage(carousel, 3, 1);

  const pageIndicator = await $('~carouselPageIndicator');
  await expect(pageIndicator).toHaveText('3 / 5');

  const activeSlide = await $('~carouselSlide[data-page="3"]');
  await expect(activeSlide).toBeDisplayed();
  await expect(activeSlide.$('img')).toHaveAttribute('alt', 'Product view 3');
});
```
Tradeoff: `scrollableElement`-scoped swipes require the element to be fully visible and not clipped by a parent `overflow: hidden` container — if the carousel is inside a `ScrollView`, UIAutomator2 may report the carousel bounds as the intersection with the visible viewport, causing `percent: 0.75` to swipe less distance than expected. Verify actual swipe coverage by logging `await carousel.getLocation()` and `await carousel.getSize()` before the swipe sequence. Also, `duration < 400` risks triggering iOS momentum scrolling that overruns the target page; always use `duration >= 500` for single-page increments.

---

**Pattern 585: Appium 2 `mobile: shell` with `adb logcat` for Real-Time Android Crash Detection During Test Execution** [community]
Relying solely on WDIO assertion failures to detect Android app crashes misses crashes that occur asynchronously (e.g., background thread ANRs, `OutOfMemoryError` in a `WorkManager` job). Running a persistent `adb logcat` shell command filtered for `AndroidRuntime FATAL EXCEPTION` and `ActivityManager: Process ... has died` in a `before`/`after` hook captures crashes that happen between commands, enabling tests to fail fast with the crash stack trace rather than a timeout error.
```typescript
import { browser } from '@wdio/globals';
import { execSync, spawn, ChildProcess } from 'child_process';

let logcatProcess: ChildProcess | null = null;
const crashLines: string[] = [];

export function startCrashMonitor(udid: string): void {
  logcatProcess = spawn('adb', [
    '-s', udid,
    'logcat',
    '-v', 'time',
    'AndroidRuntime:E',
    'ActivityManager:E',
    '*:S',
  ]);

  logcatProcess.stdout?.on('data', (chunk: Buffer) => {
    const text = chunk.toString();
    if (/FATAL EXCEPTION|has died|ANR in/.test(text)) {
      crashLines.push(text.trim());
    }
  });
}

export function stopCrashMonitor(): void {
  logcatProcess?.kill('SIGTERM');
  logcatProcess = null;
}

export function assertNoCrashes(): void {
  if (crashLines.length > 0) {
    const summary = crashLines.slice(-10).join('\n');
    crashLines.length = 0;
    throw new Error(`Android crash detected during test:\n${summary}`);
  }
  crashLines.length = 0;
}

// In wdio.conf.ts hooks:
// beforeTest: () => startCrashMonitor(capabilities['appium:udid'])
// afterTest: () => { assertNoCrashes(); stopCrashMonitor(); }

it('checkout flow completes without background crashes', async () => {
  await $('~addToCartButton').click();
  await $('~checkoutButton').click();
  await $('~confirmOrderButton').click();
  await $('~orderConfirmationScreen').waitForDisplayed({ timeout: 10000 });
  assertNoCrashes();
  await expect($('~orderNumber')).toBeDisplayed();
});
```
Tradeoff: Spawning a `logcat` process per test adds ~50 ms startup overhead and leaves a dangling process if `afterTest` is skipped on a test runner crash. Use a suite-level `before`/`after` pair instead of per-test hooks when running on CI to amortize the process startup cost. On multi-device parallel runs, each worker must pass its own `udid` to avoid cross-device log contamination. Buffer only the last 500 lines to prevent unbounded memory growth in long-running test suites.

---

**Pattern 586: XCUITest `mobile: activateApp` vs `mobile: launchApp` for Warm-Start vs Cold-Start App State Test Scenarios** [official]
Testing app behavior after a warm restart (process in memory, `applicationWillEnterForeground`) differs from a cold start (`applicationDidFinishLaunchingWithOptions`). Using `mobile: launchApp` always triggers a cold start (kills and relaunches the process), while `mobile: activateApp` brings a backgrounded app to the foreground via `UIApplication.shared.open()`. Selecting the correct command for each scenario prevents false positives where cold-start initialization masks warm-start state retention bugs.
```typescript
import { driver, browser } from '@wdio/globals';

const IOS_BUNDLE_ID = 'com.example.myapp';

async function coldStartApp(): Promise<void> {
  // Terminate the process, then launch fresh
  await driver.execute('mobile: terminateApp', { bundleId: IOS_BUNDLE_ID });
  await browser.pause(500); // Allow SpringBoard dealloc
  await driver.execute('mobile: launchApp', { bundleId: IOS_BUNDLE_ID });
}

async function warmStartApp(): Promise<void> {
  // Send to background, then bring back (warm resume)
  await driver.execute('mobile: sendAppToBackground', {
    bundleId: IOS_BUNDLE_ID,
  });
  await browser.pause(2000); // Allow OS to process backgrounding
  await driver.execute('mobile: activateApp', { bundleId: IOS_BUNDLE_ID });
}

it('cold start shows onboarding for fresh install state', async () => {
  await coldStartApp();
  const onboarding = await $('~onboardingScreen');
  await onboarding.waitForDisplayed({ timeout: 8000 });
  await expect(onboarding).toBeDisplayed();
});

it('warm start restores last viewed product tab', async () => {
  // Navigate to product tab first
  await $('~productsTabBarItem').click();
  await $('~productCard').waitForDisplayed({ timeout: 4000 });

  await warmStartApp();

  // App should restore the product tab (warm-start state retention)
  const productsTab = await $('~productsTabBarItem');
  await productsTab.waitForDisplayed({ timeout: 6000 });
  await expect(productsTab).toHaveAttr('selected', 'true');
});
```
Tradeoff: `mobile: launchApp` on XCUITest driver >= 5.0 requires `bundleId` to be specified — passing `appId` (the older capability key) is silently ignored on driver versions that migrated to the new mobile command signature. Always verify with `driver.capabilities['appium:bundleId']` that the session's bundle ID matches what you pass to these commands. Also, `mobile: activateApp` on iOS 17+ triggers the system's App Privacy Report activity log entry, which may briefly display a privacy banner overlay; add a `waitForDisplayed({ reverse: true })` guard on the banner element if it interferes with subsequent element interactions.

**Pattern 587: UIAutomator2 `mobile: type` for IME-Bypassing Fast Text Entry in Performance-Sensitive Input Fields** [official]
For text fields that use custom `InputMethodService` implementations (autocomplete, emoji keyboard overlays, password managers) or that trigger expensive real-time validation on each `KeyEvent`, `element.setValue()` and `element.sendKeys()` both inject keystrokes through the Android IME pipeline, causing each character to trigger the custom IME's `onUpdateSelection` callback. `mobile: type` bypasses the IME layer entirely, injecting text as a clipboard paste, making it 10–50x faster for long inputs and avoiding custom IME side effects.
```typescript
import { driver, $ } from '@wdio/globals';

async function typeTextFast(
  selector: string,
  text: string
): Promise<void> {
  const el = await $(selector);
  await el.click(); // Focus the field
  await driver.execute('mobile: type', { text });
}

async function typeWithValidation(
  selector: string,
  text: string,
  expectedErrorSelector?: string
): Promise<void> {
  await typeTextFast(selector, text);
  // Dismiss keyboard before asserting
  await driver.execute('mobile: hideKeyboard');

  if (expectedErrorSelector) {
    await $(expectedErrorSelector).waitForDisplayed({ timeout: 3000 });
  }
}

it('fills registration form quickly without IME side effects', async () => {
  await typeTextFast('~firstNameField', 'Jane');
  await typeTextFast('~lastNameField', 'Doe');
  await typeTextFast('~emailField', 'jane.doe@example.com');
  await typeTextFast('~passwordField', 'S3cur3P@ssw0rd!');

  await driver.execute('mobile: hideKeyboard');
  await $('~submitButton').click();
  await $('~welcomeScreen').waitForDisplayed({ timeout: 8000 });
  await expect($('~welcomeMessage')).toHaveText('Welcome, Jane!');
});

it('shows validation error for invalid email format', async () => {
  await typeWithValidation(
    '~emailField',
    'not-an-email',
    '~emailValidationError'
  );
  await expect($('~emailValidationError')).toHaveText('Enter a valid email address');
});
```
Tradeoff: `mobile: type` uses clipboard-paste injection, which overwrites the device clipboard — any content the user or a parallel test had in the clipboard is lost. On shared CI devices, this can cause interference between parallel test workers. Mitigate by reading the clipboard before (`await driver.getClipboard()`), injecting the text, and restoring afterward. Additionally, `mobile: type` does not trigger `TextWatcher.afterTextChanged()` events on some Android 13 devices when the field uses `InputFilter` — fields with strict character filters (numeric-only, max-length) may silently truncate pasted text. Verify final field value with `await el.getValue()` after typing.
